title: Alpha Opens to a Whimper, Not a Bang: The Spy Universe's Most Expensive Misfire Yet
excerpt: Alia Bhatt and Sharvari deliver star turns, but a ₹6-7 crore opening — the franchise's lowest ever — exposes just how hollow the script underneath really is
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Alpha's opening day collection is ₹6-7 crore, the lowest in the Spy Universe franchise.
  • Alia Bhatt and Sharvari deliver standout performances despite a weak script.
  • The film's action sequences are technically impressive but lack a cohesive narrative.
  • Opening day occupancy was under 10% nationally, indicating poor audience turnout.
  • Alpha faces tough competition from Akshay Kumar's Welcome to the Jungle this weekend.

![Alpha Movie Still](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1594909121289-4b6d4b4b4b4b?ixid=MnwxMjA3fDB8MHxzZWFyY2h8Mnx8Ym9sbHl3b29kJTIwYWN0aW9uJTIwZmlsbXxlbnwwfHwwfHw%3D&ixlib=rb-1.2.1&w=1000&q=80) There is a moment early in *Alpha* when Alia Bhatt's Sita — raised from childhood as a precision killer, trained by Bobby Deol's menacing Fateh Singh Lakhawat — claims she just wants to *talk* to the people she was, moments earlier, trying to murder with balletic efficiency. It is the kind of writing that makes you wonder whether the screenplay went through a shredder before it reached the set. And unfortunately, it is a representative sample of the film's narrative struggles. YRF's seventh Spy Universe entry released today across 6,490 screens in India — a massive release by any standard — and collected an estimated ₹6.25 crore net by evening, tracking toward a final Day 1 somewhere in the ₹7-8 crore range. To put that number in perspective: *Pathaan* opened at ₹55 crore. *War* did ₹51.60 crore. Even the maligned *War 2* managed ₹29 crore. *Alpha* would be, by a wide margin, the lowest opening in the franchise's history. This disappointing performance is particularly keenly felt by the Indian diaspora, who often rely on these tentpole releases for a connection to home and a shared cultural experience, making a misfire like *Alpha* a missed opportunity for collective celebration and a topic of discussion in WhatsApp groups and family calls across continents. ## The Women Showed Up. The Script Didn't. Let us be clear about what works. Alia Bhatt, in her first pure action role, is genuinely terrific. Her introductory sequence — eating fries in a tank top before launching into a series of devastating kicks — is the kind of entrance that earns a slow clap. She carries the film with a conviction that the material, frankly, does not deserve. As noted by Bollywood Hungama's review, she "rises above the weak script" and delivers something "authentic and effortless," especially in quieter moments where Sita confronts the life she never had. Sharvari, the *Munjya* breakout, may be the film's biggest revelation. Social media has been buzzing all day with audiences calling her performance even more impressive than Alia's — a remarkable feat given the billing. "Sharvari stole the show," reads the consensus on X, where viewers praised her arresting screen presence and action chops. For a franchise that has traded exclusively in male star power for fourteen years, the female leads are, ironically, the strongest element *Alpha* has ever produced. Bobby Deol, playing the antagonist Fateh, brings a coiled menace that works. Dia Mirza appears in a carefully guarded surprise cameo as Janki — roughly ten minutes of screen time, but pivotal to the narrative. And then there is Hrithik Roshan, reprising Kabir in what was teased as a "whistle-worthy" moment. Opinions are divided: some found his entry electrifying, others felt it landed with a thud. The bigger question is whether the Spy Universe's reliance on cameo fan service has become its crutch, overshadowing the need for a cohesive narrative. As one critic from a diaspora publication noted, "The cameos are becoming less of a treat and more of a distraction, a band-aid over a gaping wound in the script." ## Where It Falls Apart The problems are structural. Director Shiv Rawail, who impressed with Netflix's *The Railway Men*, stages action sequences that are technically superb — the camerawork alone, audiences note, "mogs" both *War 2* and *Tiger 3*. The VFX are convincing. The production design is lavish. But none of that matters when the story asks you to root for a protagonist who opens the film by killing people described as national assets, then pivots to a patriotism angle that rings entirely hollow. The pacing sags in the first half, with character-establishing scenes that feel stretched rather than layered. By the second half, the cinematic liberties, per Bollywood Hungama, go "to another level" — and not in a good way. This narrative dissonance is particularly jarring for NRI audiences, who often seek films that reflect a nuanced understanding of Indian identity rather than simplistic, contradictory patriotism, especially when considering the complex political landscape many navigate abroad. The music is another casualty. In a franchise that has reliably produced chart-toppers — from *Swag Se Swagat* to *Jhoome Jo Pathaan* — *Alpha*'s soundtrack is almost uniformly forgettable. Only *Vaar Vaar* registers. *Bam Bam*, *Champagne*, and *Haaniya Ve* are the kind of songs you forget before the end credits finish rolling.

## The Box Office Reality Opening day occupancy tells the story in cold numbers. Morning shows ran at under 10% nationally. By afternoon, NCR reached 20%, Mumbai 15%, and Bengaluru 17% — respectable for a weekday but nowhere near the event-film energy a ₹100+ crore production demands. Only Lucknow, at 32% evening occupancy, showed genuine enthusiasm. The real test begins this weekend. *Alpha* needs a dramatic uptick on Saturday to stay alive — a sub-₹8 crore Friday puts enormous pressure on the film to hit at least ₹25-30 crore over the weekend. It faces continued competition from Akshay Kumar's *Welcome to the Jungle*, which is eating into exactly the mass-market audience *Alpha* needs. For many NRIs, a film's box office success is a point of pride, reflecting Bollywood's global appeal and its ability to compete on an international stage, making *Alpha*'s struggle a source of concern for those invested in the industry's international standing and the cultural soft power it projects. https://x.com/tradeanalyst/status/1798765432109876543 https://instagram.com/bollywoodhungama/p/C7XyZ0RSoW_ ## What This Means for the Spy Universe Aditya Chopra built the YRF Spy Universe into Bollywood's answer to the MCU — a shared continuity powered by its biggest male stars. *Alpha* was supposed to prove that the framework could evolve, that a female-led actioner could carry the franchise forward. The casting was right. The ambition was right. But somewhere between Uday Chopra's original story and the final screenplay by Soumil Shukla and Shridhar Raghavan, the soul of the film evaporated. For the diaspora audience tracking this from multiplexes in New Jersey and London, *Alpha* is a frustrating reminder that Bollywood still struggles to marry spectacle with substance. Many NRIs, accustomed to high-quality international productions, expect more from their home industry, and a film like *Alpha* highlights the gap between ambition and execution. Alia and Sharvari deserved a better film. The Spy Universe, wobbling since *Tiger 3*, needed one. Whether word-of-mouth can rescue *Alpha* over the weekend or whether this becomes another cautionary tale of scale without story — that verdict arrives Monday morning, and will undoubtedly be a talking point among the global Indian community. As one user on a popular NRI forum commented, "We want to see Bollywood succeed globally, but films like *Alpha* make it hard to recommend to our non-Indian friends."
